title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop affects verifier-detected safety violations for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified into VLAN-change = 167, ACL-change = 167, static-route-change = 166) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test (archived executor convention) returned two-sided p = 1.00 for the observed discordant counts. Notably, the guarded loop performed one repair that converted a single baseline failure into a verified pass (discordant pair_id = pair-000317; archived validator_trace and repair trace summarized in Results). Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; measured marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks: intent-to-configuration translation, change planning, and automated repair. Operational safety in these settings typically depends on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms—rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A common operational architecture is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM proposes a candidate configuration; a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties; automated repairs or human review follow if violations are detected. Despite conceptual consensus on the need for guardrails, controlled measurements that isolate the marginal contribution of a verifier (holding the LLM proposal fixed) are scarce. Practitioners need to know: when an LLM already produces high-quality candidates, how much incremental safety does a verifier plus a modest automated repair budget provide on a verifier-scoped pass/fail metric? To address this, we preregistered and executed a paired, artifact-backed experiment that isolates verifier+repair impact under canonical, deterministic semantics.
sections.related_work: Deterministic verification tools and header-space / route-model analyzers provide machine-checkable properties (reachability, isolation, update atomicity) and motivate verifier-in-the-loop system designs [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps systems integrate LLMs for intent parsing and configuration generation while emphasizing engineering guardrails (e.g., INTA, Confucius, and others) [INTA, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair patterns are proposed across structured-generation domains to reduce unsafe outputs [PoeTone; INTA]. Parallel literature documents LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors) and recommends verification/human oversight as mitigations [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. Our study contributes a preregistered, artifact-backed paired measurement that isolates verifier+single-repair impact while keeping the LLM’s initial proposal identical for both arms.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026 and froze the research question, task generator seeds, inclusion/exclusion rules, estimands, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule before execution. Primary confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM producing an unvalidated single proposal (paired within-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. The preregistration and artifacts are archived (preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the execution manifest).

Task corpus and strata. A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using frozen seeds. Tasks were stratified into three preregistered clusters: VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), static-route-change (166); the realized allocation matches the preregistered allocation and is recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (manifest archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl; complete_pair_count = 500 in deterministic_reconciliation.json). Generator constraints restricted allowed_features to {admin, mtu, vlan} to align with the deterministic verifier’s modeled scope; tasks referencing unmodeled features were excluded per preregistration (no such exclusions occurred in this run).

Generation semantics and adapter. To isolate the verifier’s marginal effect we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false). For each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal; that identical candidate served both as the baseline proposal and as the input to the guarded verifier. The guarded arm invoked the registered repair-stage provider call only if the determinant verifier reported a preregistered high- or medium-severity violation on the shared candidate. Requested model = gpt-5-mini called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (execution/model_configuration.json archived). Deterministic verifier = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator-spec and violation-code→severity mapping archived). The guarded path permitted at most one automated repair iteration as preregistered.

Outcome definition, tests, and inference. Primary outcome per task: binary pass/fail of verifier-detected safety-violation (pass == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Primary confirmatory test: an exact McNemar two-sided test implemented by the archived analysis_executor as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01; see analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute difference were computed with B = 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), resampling at the task/pair unit while preserving pairing. Missingness/retry rules followed the preregistered contract (up to two automated retries for transient provider errors; sensitivity treatments archived). Stopping rule: stop after processing all preregistered confirmatory pairs or when adapter maximum_model_calls reached; execution recorded model_calls_used = 501 and completed_episode_count = 1000.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729) as archived in analysis artifacts. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p (executor’s exact-binomial-on-discordant-rounding convention) = 1.00 for the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1).

Discordant episode: deterministic identifier and sanitizer summary. Per the reviewer request, we include the deterministic pair identifier and a short artifact-backed summary of the single corrected episode. Discordant episode pair_id = pair-000317 (recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl and referenced by deterministic_reconciliation.json). Archived validator_trace for pair-000317 shows the baseline shared candidate incurred a medium-severity verifier violation categorized under the verifier taxonomy as a "workflow_precondition_violation" (the verifier flagged a missing required precondition: the device-admin field had to be set to down prior to changing MTU/VLAN). The guarded pipeline issued one automated repair-stage call that inserted the missing precondition command (a single 'admin down' command on the affected interface) before the change sequence. After applying that single repair the deterministic verifier reported zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations and the pair was scored as a pass under the archived scoring rule (repair_applied = true). All per-task validator_trace fields, the repair prompt/response (sanitized to configuration commands), and provider-call traces for pair-000317 are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/provider_calls/* and may be deterministically retrieved; the above short summary is extracted verbatim from those archived traces. The run-level reconciliation and provider-call audit confirm exactly one repair-stage call and exactly one discordant pair (see deterministic_reconciliation.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Secondary analyses and power considerations. The preregistration assumed baseline error prevalence ≈ 0.30 to size N for 80% power to detect an absolute 0.10 reduction. Observed baseline failure prevalence (1/500) produced a ceiling effect that materially reduced power to detect small absolute improvements on the composite pass/fail metric; consequently secondary per-violation-class analyses were uninformative due to near-zero counts. All diagnostics (missingness_summary.csv, contamination_summary.csv) show no exclusions and zero failed episodes under the execution contract.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications. Under the constrained experimental regime—single requested LLM (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic verifier modeling a limited feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and at most one automated repair iteration—the LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This is a conditional, operationally meaningful result: when baseline proposal quality is very high for the verifier-modeled properties, modest verifier+repair budgets may offer small incremental pass-rate gains on a composite binary metric. Nonetheless, the verifier demonstrated concrete utility by converting one baseline failure into a pass in the guarded arm (pair-000317).

Design-choice consequences. Our shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate verifier+repair impact conditional on identical proposals; this choice answers deployment scenarios where regeneration cost is constrained or where an operator prefers repairing a single human-reviewed proposal. Alternative semantics—verifier-guided regeneration, iterative repairs, or multiple repair iterations—could yield larger absolute improvements at increased model-call cost; these alternatives require separate preregistrations and cost–benefit analyses.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic task seeds, and automated replacement rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity is limited by the verifier’s coverage: pass==no preregistered high/medium-severity violations is defined relative to the verifier’s modeled properties and severity mapping (validator-spec archived). If production operators require properties outside that modeled set (vendor-specific CLI semantics, dynamic protocol states), the measured pass-rate difference here underestimates potential verifier benefit. External validity is constrained by single-model testing, a synthetic task corpus, and the verifier’s limited feature set; we do not claim multi-model or cross-vendor generality.

Statistical nuance. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the executor’s exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs computation and the empirical discordant counts (n = 1). With so few discordants, small-sample exact p-values can be non-intuitive; the paired-bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.006] complements the exact test by quantifying plausible absolute differences. Practitioners must interpret effect sizes against baseline error prevalence: extremely low baseline error produces ceiling effects that limit detectability of modest verifier-driven improvements.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) isolating the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the run’s exact-binomial convention). This conditional measurement illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high for the verifier-modeled properties and verifier coverage is limited, the measurable marginal pass-rate benefit of a modest verifier+repair budget can be small on a composite pass/fail metric, although the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures (e.g., pair-000317). We recommend practitioners (1) measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative data before allocating repair budgets, (2) align verifier coverage with operator-critical properties, and (3) select generation semantics (shared initial vs verifier-guided regeneration) consistent with deployment cost and safety priorities. The full preregistration, code, prompts, model outputs, validator traces (including the pair-000317 repair trace), provider-call logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection of every claim made here.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (pair-000317) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where the baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while the guarded scoring outcome indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns pair-000317 and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
